title: Attention Variants and Flash Attention
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Attention Variants and Flash Attention ##### The GPU that spent 92% of its time waiting A team serving a 7B model in Hyderabad benchmarked their inference stack and found something that made no sense. Their A100 reported 8% utilisation of its tensor cores during generation, yet throughput was pinned — adding requests just increased latency. They were not compute-bound. They were **memory-bandwidth bound**, and the culprit was the KV cache. At 8K context, batch 32, their MHA model's KV cache was 42 GB. Every single generated token required reading that entire cache from HBM into the compute units. An A100's HBM bandwidth is about 2 TB/s, so 42 GB per token means roughly 21 ms of pure memory traffic before any arithmetic happens. They switched to a GQA checkpoint with 8 KV heads instead of 32. The cache dropped to 10.5 GB. Throughput went up 3.4×, and tensor core utilisation rose to 31%. **Modern attention engineering is almost entirely about memory, not FLOPs.** Standard attention is not slow because the matrix multiplications are expensive — it is slow because it reads and writes enormous intermediate tensors to slow memory. Flash Attention and GQA are two different attacks on that same problem, and understanding both is what lets you reason about inference cost. ##### The memory hierarchy The fact that makes everything else make sense: | Memory | Size (A100) | Bandwidth | Relative speed | |---|---|---|---| | SRAM (on-chip) | 20 MB | ~19 TB/s | 1× | | HBM (GPU RAM) | 40–80 GB | ~2 TB/s | ~10× slower | | CPU RAM | 100s GB | ~100 GB/s | ~200× slower | SRAM is roughly ten times faster than HBM and four thousand times smaller. **An operation that touches HBM repeatedly is slow regardless of how few FLOPs it performs.** This gives us the concept of **arithmetic intensity** — FLOPs performed per byte moved. Matrix multiplication has high intensity and saturates the tensor cores. Softmax, dropout, and elementwise operations have intensity near 1 and are pure memory traffic. Standard attention is a sandwich of high-intensity matmuls around low-intensity elementwise operations, and the elementwise parts dominate the wall clock. ##### Why standard attention is memory-bound ```python # Standard attention, written the obvious way S = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(d_k) # write (B,h,N,N) to HBM S = S.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf")) # read + write (B,h,N,N) P = torch.softmax(S, dim=-1) # read + write (B,h,N,N) P = dropout(P) # read + write (B,h,N,N) O = P @ V # read (B,h,N,N) ``` Count the traffic on that `(B, h, N, N)` tensor. For batch 8, 32 heads, 4096 context, fp16: ```python B, h, N = 8, 32, 4096 bytes_per_matrix = B * h * N * N * 2 print(f"{bytes_per_matrix / 1e9:.1f} GB per intermediate") # 8.6 GB ``` 8.6 GB, written and read roughly four times = ~34 GB of HBM traffic, for one attention layer, on one forward pass. At 2 TB/s that is 17 ms of pure memory movement. The actual matmul FLOPs would take about 2 ms on the tensor cores. ##### Flash Attention Dao et al. (2022) observed that **you never need to materialise the full attention matrix.** The technique is tiling plus online softmax. Load blocks of Q, K, and V into SRAM, compute the attention for that block, and accumulate the output incrementally — never writing the `N×N` matrix to HBM at all. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Q, K, V in HBM"] --> B["Load block of Q
into SRAM"] B --> C["Loop over blocks of K, V"] C --> D["Compute S_block = Q_b @ K_b^T
in SRAM"] D --> E["Online softmax:
update running max & sum"] E --> F["Accumulate O_block += P_block @ V_b"] F --> C C -->|"all blocks done"| G["Write O block to HBM
ONCE"] G --> B H["N×N matrix
NEVER written to HBM"] -.-> D ``` The mathematical trick is the **online softmax**: you can compute a numerically stable softmax in a streaming fashion by tracking a running maximum and a running sum, rescaling previous partial results when a new maximum appears. ```python def online_softmax_accumulate(m_prev, l_prev, o_prev, s_block, v_block): """One step of the Flash Attention accumulation.""" m_new = torch.maximum(m_prev, s_block.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values) # Rescale the previous accumulation to the new maximum correction = torch.exp(m_prev - m_new) p_block = torch.exp(s_block - m_new) l_new = correction * l_prev + p_block.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) o_new = correction * o_prev + p_block @ v_block return m_new, l_new, o_new ``` **The results:** memory drops from O(N²) to O(N), and wall-clock speeds up 2–4× — despite Flash Attention performing *more* FLOPs (it recomputes the attention matrix during the backward pass rather than storing it). Trading compute for memory traffic is a win when you are bandwidth-bound. It is **exact**, not approximate. The output is numerically identical to standard attention up to floating-point reordering. In PyTorch it is one function: ```python import torch.nn.functional as F # Automatically dispatches to Flash Attention when the inputs qualify out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention( q, k, v, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0 if not training else 0.1, is_causal=True, # use this rather than a materialised mask ) ``` **`is_causal=True` matters.** Passing an explicit `(N, N)` boolean mask forces the fallback path, because Flash Attention handles causality implicitly by skipping blocks above the diagonal. That one argument is often the difference between getting Flash Attention and silently not getting it. Check which backend fired: ```python from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel with sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION): out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) # Raises if Flash cannot be used — useful for verifying in CI ``` Requirements for the Flash path: fp16 or bf16, head dimension ≤ 256, no arbitrary attention bias, and an Ampere-or-newer GPU. ##### The KV cache During autoregressive generation, keys and values for previous tokens do not change. Recomputing them every step is O(N²) work per token; caching makes it O(N). The cost is memory, and it is the dominant memory cost in serving: $$\text{KV cache bytes} = 2 \times B \times N \times L \times n_{kv} \times d_{head} \times \text{bytes}$$ ```python def kv_cache_gb(batch, seq_len, n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2): return 2 * batch * seq_len * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes / 1e9 # Llama-2 7B: 32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim 128 print(f"MHA 8k ctx, batch 32: {kv_cache_gb(32, 8192, 32, 32, 128):.1f} GB") # 42.9 print(f"GQA 8k ctx, batch 32: {kv_cache_gb(32, 8192, 32, 8, 128):.1f} GB") # 10.7 print(f"MQA 8k ctx, batch 32: {kv_cache_gb(32, 8192, 32, 1, 128):.1f} GB") # 1.3 ``` Those three numbers are the Hyderabad story. The model weights are 14 GB; the MHA cache at batch 32 is three times the model. And critically, **during decoding you read the entire cache for every single token.** Generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound — which is why the tensor cores sat at 8%. ##### MHA, MQA, GQA ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph MHA["MHA — 8 Q heads, 8 KV heads"] Q1["Q1"] --> K1["K1,V1"] Q2["Q2"] --> K2["K2,V2"] Q3["Q3"] --> K3["K3,V3"] Q4["Q4"] --> K4["K4,V4"] end subgraph GQA["GQA — 8 Q heads, 2 KV heads"] G1["Q1"] --> GK1["K1,V1"] G2["Q2"] --> GK1 G3["Q3"] --> GK2["K2,V2"] G4["Q4"] --> GK2 end subgraph MQA["MQA — 8 Q heads, 1 KV head"] M1["Q1"] --> MK["K,V"] M2["Q2"] --> MK M3["Q3"] --> MK M4["Q4"] --> MK end ``` **MQA** (Shazeer, 2019) shares one K/V head across all query heads. Maximum cache reduction, but a measurable quality drop and training instability at scale. **GQA** (Ainslie et al., 2023) groups query heads to share K/V heads — the interpolation between the two. With 32 query heads and 8 KV heads you get a 4× cache reduction and quality statistically indistinguishable from MHA. **GQA is the industry default**: Llama-2 70B, Llama-3 (all sizes), Mistral, Mixtral, Qwen2, and Gemma all use it. The typical ratio is 4:1 or 8:1. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GroupedQueryAttention(nn.Module): def __init__(self, d_model=4096, n_heads=32, n_kv_heads=8, max_seq=8192): super().__init__() assert n_heads % n_kv_heads == 0 self.n_heads, self.n_kv_heads = n_heads, n_kv_heads self.n_rep = n_heads // n_kv_heads # queries per KV head self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads self.wq = nn.Linear(d_model, n_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False) self.wk = nn.Linear(d_model, n_kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False) self.wv = nn.Linear(d_model, n_kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False) self.wo = nn.Linear(n_heads * self.head_dim, d_model, bias=False) @staticmethod def _repeat_kv(x, n_rep): """(B, n_kv, N, hd) -> (B, n_kv*n_rep, N, hd) without copying memory.""" if n_rep == 1: return x B, n_kv, N, hd = x.shape return (x[:, :, None, :, :] .expand(B, n_kv, n_rep, N, hd) .reshape(B, n_kv * n_rep, N, hd)) def forward(self, x, kv_cache=None): B, N, _ = x.shape q = self.wq(x).view(B, N, self.n_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2) k = self.wk(x).view(B, N, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2) v = self.wv(x).view(B, N, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2) if kv_cache is not None: k = torch.cat([kv_cache["k"], k], dim=2) v = torch.cat([kv_cache["v"], v], dim=2) kv_cache["k"], kv_cache["v"] = k, v # store the SMALL tensors k = self._repeat_kv(k, self.n_rep) # expand only for the matmul v = self._repeat_kv(v, self.n_rep) out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=(kv_cache is None)) out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, N, -1) return self.wo(out) ``` **The key implementation detail** is in `_repeat_kv`: you cache the small `n_kv_heads` tensors and expand only transiently for the matmul. `expand` creates a view without copying, so the memory saving is real. Caching the expanded tensors would defeat the entire purpose — and it is a genuinely common bug. | | MHA | GQA (4:1) | MQA | |---|---|---|---| | KV cache | 1× | 0.25× | 1/32× | | Quality | Baseline | ≈ baseline | −1 to −2 pts | | Training stability | Good | Good | Can be unstable | | Used by | GPT-3, Llama-1 | **Llama-2/3, Mistral, Qwen** | PaLM, Falcon-7B | **MLA** (Multi-head Latent Attention), introduced in DeepSeek-V2, goes further by compressing K/V into a low-rank latent and reconstructing per head — reportedly better quality than GQA at a smaller cache. Worth watching. ##### The quadratic problem Attention is O(N²·d) in compute and, without Flash, O(N²) in memory. Flash removes the memory term; the compute term remains. ```python def attention_flops(seq_len, d_model, n_layers): return 4 * n_layers * seq_len * seq_len * d_model # QK^T and PV for n in [2048, 8192, 32768, 131072]: f = attention_flops(n, 4096, 32) print(f"{n:>7,} ctx: {f/1e12:>8.1f} TFLOPs") # 131,072 ctx is 4096× the cost of 2,048 ``` That is why 128K context is an engineering achievement rather than a config change. Approaches that reduce it: sliding-window attention (Mistral — each token attends to the last 4096, with information propagating across layers), sparse patterns (Longformer, BigBird), and linear-attention variants (Performer, RWKV, Mamba) that trade exactness for O(N). **Ring Attention** and sequence parallelism shard the sequence across GPUs, enabling million-token contexts — with all-to-all communication as the new bottleneck. ##### Benchmarking properly ```python import torch, time import torch.nn.functional as F from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel def bench_attention(seq_lens, batch=4, n_heads=32, head_dim=128, iters=20): device = "cuda" rows = [] for N in seq_lens: q, k, v = (torch.randn(batch, n_heads, N, head_dim, device=device, dtype=torch.float16) for _ in range(3)) for name, backend in [("math", SDPBackend.MATH), ("flash", SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION)]: try: torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats() with sdpa_kernel(backend): for _ in range(3): # warm-up F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) torch.cuda.synchronize() t0 = time.perf_counter() for _ in range(iters): F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) torch.cuda.synchronize() dt = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / iters * 1000 rows.append({"seq": N, "backend": name, "ms": round(dt, 2), "peak_GB": round(torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()/1e9, 2)}) except RuntimeError as exc: rows.append({"seq": N, "backend": name, "ms": None, "peak_GB": None, "error": str(exc)[:60]}) return rows ``` **Three benchmarking rules:** always warm up (the first CUDA call includes kernel compilation), always `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before timing (CUDA is asynchronous and you will otherwise measure launch overhead), and report peak memory alongside latency, because memory is usually the binding constraint. At short sequences Flash and math will be close. Past about 2048 the gap widens sharply, and the math backend will OOM where Flash keeps going. ##### Common mistakes - **Passing an explicit mask instead of `is_causal=True`**, silently disabling Flash Attention. - **Caching the expanded GQA K/V tensors**, negating the memory saving. - **Benchmarking without warm-up or synchronisation.** - **Assuming Flash Attention changes the result.** It is exact. - **Sizing GPU memory from model weights** and forgetting the KV cache — the 42 GB surprise. - **Using fp32**, which disqualifies the Flash kernel entirely. - **Head dimension above 256**, which also disqualifies it. - **Reporting tensor core utilisation** as if it measured efficiency during memory-bound decoding. - **Choosing MQA for quality-sensitive work** when GQA costs almost nothing extra. - **Ignoring prefill versus decode.** Prefill is compute-bound and parallel; decode is memory-bound and sequential. They need different optimisations. - **Not checking that your serving framework enables paged KV cache** — vLLM's PagedAttention typically doubles throughput by eliminating cache fragmentation. ##### Hands-on: measure the crossover Your practical task benchmarks standard versus Flash Attention across sequence lengths, plotting latency and memory. Use the harness above and sweep 512 through 16384. Plot both on log axes. You will see the math backend's memory curve bend upward quadratically and terminate in an OOM, while Flash's stays linear — that pair of curves is the clearest single illustration of what Flash Attention bought the field. The mini project implements GQA and measures the cache reduction and quality impact against MHA. Train two small models with identical parameter counts (increase `d_model` slightly for GQA to compensate for the smaller K/V projections) on the same data. Report validation perplexity and KV cache size at a few context lengths. The expected finding — a 4× cache reduction for well under a point of perplexity — is worth confirming with your own numbers. The assignment analyses why GQA is the industry default, with a KV cache calculation for a 7B model at 8K context. Show the arithmetic for MHA, GQA at 4:1, and MQA; then connect it to serving economics — how many concurrent requests fit on one A100 under each scheme, and what that does to cost per token. That link from architecture choice to rupees per million tokens is exactly the reasoning a senior engineer is expected to make. ##### Key takeaways - **Attention is memory-bound, not compute-bound.** Standard attention writes an `N×N` tensor to HBM four times, and that traffic dominates the wall clock. - **Flash Attention tiles the computation in SRAM with an online softmax**, achieving O(N) memory and 2–4× speedup while remaining numerically exact. - **The KV cache is often larger than the model** and must be read in full for every generated token, which is why decoding saturates bandwidth rather than tensor cores. - **GQA is the default because it cuts the cache 4–8× for negligible quality loss** — cache the small K/V tensors and expand only for the matmul. - **Prefill and decode are different regimes**: prefill is parallel and compute-bound, decode is sequential and memory-bound, and they call for different optimisations.
practical_task_reference: Benchmark standard attention vs Flash Attention (via PyTorch SDPA) on increasing sequence lengths and plot latency and memory.
